passage:
On Sunday night, in their Mumbai flat, Vaibhav sat on the bed and repeated the Hindi poem forty times for Monday's recitation. By ten o'clock the words came out smoothly. "Done!" Vaibhav told Indu didi.
On Monday the recitation went well.
On Friday the teacher said, "Surprise! Say it again for parents' day." Vaibhav stood up, said the first line and froze. The rest had gone, like chalk wiped off a board.
At home Indu didi smiled. "When I learn poems, I say them for ten minutes a day, for five days. It feels slow, but they stay."
Vaibhav frowned, then took the book out again. "Ten minutes. Starting today."

qa.q: How many times did Vaibhav repeat the poem on Sunday night?
qa.a: Vaibhav repeated it forty times.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav feel "Done!" on Sunday night?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt confident and relieved because the words were coming out smoothly by ten o'clock, so the poem felt learned, even though it had all been packed into one evening.

qa.q: What does Indu didi suggest, and why does it work better?
qa.a: Ten minutes a day for five days; spreading it out makes the poem stay, even if it feels slower.

qa.q: What might the teacher think on seeing Vaibhav freeze on Friday?
qa.a: The teacher may be surprised, since Monday went well, and may guess the poem was crammed rather than truly learned.

grounding: It shows a child who learns a poem in one evening, recites it the next day and loses it within days.

passage:
"Himani, dinner!"
"One more time, Mummy. I'll say the poem fifty times tonight."
"The competition is next week."
"I'll learn it all tonight, so I'm free after."
Three days later:
"Say it for Nani on the phone, Himani."
"'The river runs...' um. 'The river runs...' Mummy, it's gone!"
"All of it?"
"Only the first line is left." Himani's lip wobbled.
Sarita, her mother, sat down beside her. "Remember when I learned the road signs for my driving test? A few every night for a week, and I still know them."
"So... a little every day?"
"A little every day. And tomorrow, try saying it before you open the book."
Himani wiped her eyes. "Okay. Five minutes tonight."

qa.q: What was all that was left of the poem after three days?
qa.a: Only the first line was left.

qa.q: Why did Himani want to learn the whole poem in one night?
qa.a: Himani wanted to be free for the rest of the week, and saying it fifty times in one night felt like it would lock it in.

qa.q: What small step did Himani and Sarita agree on?
qa.a: Five minutes a day, trying to say the poem before opening the book.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel watching Himani's lip wobble?
qa.a: Sarita probably feels sympathy and wants to help rather than scold, which is why she shares her own road-sign story.

grounding: It shows a child who crams a poem in one evening and loses it within days, then tries learning a little each day.

passage:
Last year I thought I was a poem champion. The night before the recitation, I read the river poem over and over till midnight. Next morning I said every line perfectly.
A week later Arohi asked me to say it with her for fun. I got two lines in and stopped. Arohi, who had practised a little every day for two weeks, went all the way to the end.
I was annoyed, but I asked her how. She said, "I just said it at breakfast and at bedtime. Small bits."
This year, for the new poem, I tried her way. Ten minutes every evening. Last week I said it for my Nana, a whole month after the recitation. I'm Hansa, and I'm still a little proud.

qa.q: How long did Hansa read the poem the night before the recitation?
qa.a: Hansa read it over and over till midnight.

qa.q: Why was Hansa annoyed when Arohi finished the poem?
qa.a: Hansa had felt like a poem champion after a perfect recitation, so forgetting it a week later while Arohi remembered it felt unfair.

qa.q: What choice did Hansa make for the new poem, and what happened?
qa.a: Hansa tried Arohi's way, ten minutes every evening, and could still say it for Nana a whole month later. 🎉

qa.q: How might Arohi feel when Hansa asks how she did it?
qa.a: Arohi may feel pleased to share a simple trick, and glad Hansa asked instead of staying annoyed.

grounding: It shows a child whose poem, crammed in one night, faded within a week, while a friend's daily practice lasted.

passage: Class teacher's note, Class 4B, Tamarind Road School. Kavitha (age 9) was chosen to recite a poem at Friday's assembly. On Monday morning she said all sixteen lines to me without one mistake. She told me proudly she had learned the whole thing in one evening, "saying it again and again till dinner." On Thursday, at the practice, she stopped after line four. She tried twice more and her lip trembled. "But Miss, I knew it!" she said. I believe she did, on Monday. I took the poem and cut it into four strips of four lines. We agreed she would say one strip each morning with her Amma, and the next strip the day after, then all of them at the end of the week. The assembly moved to next Friday. I'll write again then. — Shalini

qa.q: How many lines did Kavitha say without a mistake on Monday morning?
qa.a: She said all sixteen lines without one mistake.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she said, "But Miss, I knew it!"
qa.a: She felt confused and upset 😢 because the poem had felt solid on Monday, so losing it by Thursday seemed unfair.

qa.q: What new plan did Shalini make, and why might it work better than one long evening?
qa.a: Splitting the poem into strips and practising one each morning spreads the learning over days, so it has time to settle instead of fading.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's Amma be part of the change?
qa.a: Amma becomes the morning practice partner, so learning becomes a small daily habit at home rather than one tiring night.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child who learned a poem in one evening losing it within days, and a plan to spread practice out.

passage:
Wednesday
Dear diary, I am so annoyed. On Saturday night I learned the whole poem for the annual day audition. I said it twenty times, maybe thirty. I was perfect. Nani clapped.
Today at lunch Sumit said, "Test?" and held the paper. I did the first verse fine. Then my brain went white, like a blank board. Sumit had to whisper the middle lines. HOW?? It was all inside my head on Saturday!
Nani says learning is like watering her tulsi plant. If you pour a whole bucket once, most of it runs out. A little every day stays. I think she might be right, which is also annoying.
The audition is on Monday. I'm going to say one verse at breakfast, one at bedtime, and let Sumit test me in the bus every day.
Mridul

qa.q: When did Mridul learn the whole poem?
qa.a: On Saturday night, for the annual day audition.

qa.q: How can you tell Mridul felt frustrated about forgetting?
qa.a: Mridul writes "I am so annoyed" and "HOW??", and remembers being perfect on Saturday, which makes the blank feel unfair.

qa.q: What plan did Mridul choose for the days before Monday?
qa.a: Saying one verse at breakfast and one at bedtime, and letting Sumit test on the bus every day, which spreads the practice out.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sumit to whisper the middle lines?
qa.a: Sumit is trying to help a friend and may feel a bit awkward, but also useful, and now gets to be the daily tester.

grounding: A child's diary shows a poem learned in one evening fading within days, and a new plan to practise a little each day.

passage:
Monday
Disaster. On Thursday night I learned the whole poem, 'The Rain Song', all sixteen lines, in one evening. Ammi tested me three times before bed and I got it perfect. On Friday I recited it in class without a single mistake and got a star.
Today Ma'am asked the winners to recite again at assembly. I stood up, got to line five and... nothing. Blank. My face burned. Pema, who learned hers a few lines a day all last week, said hers perfectly again.
At lunch Pema said she practises a bit every day, even after the test. I thought learning it once perfectly was enough. It isn't.
For the next poem, I'm doing four lines a day, and saying the old lines too.
Rehana

qa.q: How many lines were in 'The Rain Song'?
qa.a: Sixteen lines.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when the poem went blank at assembly?
qa.a: Rehana felt embarrassed and shocked, face burning, because the poem learned perfectly on Thursday had already faded by Monday.

qa.q: What is Rehana's plan for the next poem, and why is it better?
qa.a: Four lines a day while repeating the old lines, spreading the learning out so it lasts longer.

qa.q: How did Pema learn her poem differently?
qa.a: Pema learned a few lines a day all week and kept practising after the test, so it stayed.

passage: At the village school in Barshi, the teacher announced a tables test for Friday. Gautam spent Thursday night under the lantern shouting twelves and thirteens until his mother begged him to stop. On Friday he wrote every answer right. By the next Wednesday, when the teacher asked him thirteen sevens, he couldn't find it anywhere in his head. His friend Santosh answered at once. Santosh had practised a few tables every evening while grazing the goats, saying them to the goats all week, and then again on Sunday for fun. "The goats know them now too," he joked. Gautam didn't laugh. He had worked so hard on Thursday. That evening he went along with Santosh and the goats and said the thirteens again, and again the next day.

qa.q: What did Santosh do while grazing the goats?
qa.a: He practised a few tables every evening, saying them to the goats.

qa.q: Why didn't Gautam laugh at Santosh's joke?
qa.a: Gautam felt frustrated and let down, having worked so hard on Thursday night only to forget the tables within days.

qa.q: What did Gautam start doing, and why should it help?
qa.a: Saying the thirteens with Santosh each evening, spreading practice over days so the tables last.

qa.q: How does Santosh feel about the tables?
qa.a: Santosh feels relaxed and confident, joking that even the goats know them now.

grounding: Shows a child who crammed tables in one night forgetting them within days, while a friend who practised daily remembers.

passage: In Seville, Mina had two weeks to learn her lines for the school play: twenty lines as the Wise Owl. She ignored them until the first Sunday, then learned them all in one long afternoon, reciting to her grandmother until she was word-perfect. At Monday's rehearsal she was brilliant. By Friday's dress rehearsal, the lines had leaked away like water from a cupped hand. She stood on stage in her feather cape, mouth open. Ines, playing the Fox, whispered the first words from the side. Ines had learned her lines a few each day on the walk to school, and went over them again every morning. Afterwards Mina asked how. "Little bits, lots of days," Ines said. The next week, Mina did ten minutes a day with her grandmother, and on the night, the Owl didn't miss a word.

qa.q: What part did Mina play?
qa.a: The Wise Owl.

qa.q: How did Mina feel standing on stage at the dress rehearsal?
qa.a: Mina felt panicked and embarrassed, mouth open, as the lines learned in one afternoon leaked away.

qa.q: What did Mina change, and why did it work?
qa.a: She practised ten minutes a day with her grandmother, spreading the learning out so the lines stayed until the night.

qa.q: How did Ines help Mina, and how had Ines learned?
qa.a: Ines whispered the first words from the side, having learned the lines a few each day and reviewed them every morning.

grounding: Shows a child who learned lines in one afternoon forgetting them within days, and remembering once practice is spread out.

passage:
In the school hall, Bidisha, nine, recited the poem for the class competition perfectly on Friday. She had learnt it the night before, all twelve lines, repeating them until midnight.

On Monday, her teacher Naveen sir asked her to recite it again for the parents' visit.

Bidisha stood up. "The river runs... the river runs..." She couldn't remember the second line. Her face went hot.

Naveen sir smiled kindly. "You learnt it all in one night, didn't you?"

She nodded, eyes stinging.

"Try five minutes a day for a week next time. It'll stay."

That week she practised the new poem a little each day. The next month, she could still say every line.

qa.q: How many lines did the poem have?
qa.a: Twelve lines.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when she forgot the second line?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and upset, with her face hot and her eyes stinging.

qa.q: What did Naveen sir suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: He suggested five minutes a day for a week, which helped the poem stay in her memory much longer.

qa.q: How might Naveen sir have felt when Bidisha forgot the line?
qa.a: Naveen sir likely felt sympathetic and wanted to help her learn a better way.

grounding: A child who learns a poem all in one night forgets it within days, and spreading practice out helps it stay.

passage:
Tuesday. Varun, ten, had a poem to recite on Friday. He left it till Thursday night and repeated it forty times. His sister Neelam covered her ears.

Friday. He recited it perfectly and got a gold star.

The next Wednesday. The teacher asked for the poem again at assembly. Varun remembered the first two lines and then nothing. He mumbled and sat down, cheeks burning.

The Saturday after. Neelam said, "Try this with the next poem: read it every day, just a few times." Varun grumbled but tried it, reading his new poem at breakfast each morning.

Three weeks later, he could still say it, word for word.

qa.q: How many times did Varun repeat the poem on Thursday night?
qa.a: Forty times.

qa.q: How did Varun feel when he forgot the poem at assembly?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, with his cheeks burning, because he had known it perfectly only days before.

qa.q: What did Neelam suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: She suggested reading the poem a few times every day, which helped Varun remember it for weeks.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel when Varun still remembers the new poem?
qa.a: Neelam probably feels pleased and a little proud of her advice.

grounding: A child who crams a poem in one evening forgets it in days, while spreading practice out makes it stick.

passage:
Kiran, you want to learn your poem in one night? Let your Tanvir dadu tell you something.

When I was ten, in our village school, I had to recite a long poem at the Independence Day function. I learnt it all the night before by the lantern. My mother kept saying, "Go to sleep," and I kept saying, "Just once more."

The next morning, I stood on the stage and said it perfectly. Everyone clapped.

But a week later, my teacher asked me to recite it for the inspector. I could not remember even the third line. I stood there, silent, while everyone looked at me.

After that, my teacher made me read my poems for ten minutes every morning, for many days. Those poems, Kiran, I still remember.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir learn the poem the night before?
qa.a: By the lantern.

qa.q: How did young Tanvir feel standing silent in front of the inspector?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and embarrassed, since everyone was looking at him and he couldn't remember the poem.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Tanvir remember poems for life?
qa.a: His teacher made him read poems for ten minutes every morning for many days, instead of cramming.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's teacher have felt when he couldn't recite for the inspector?
qa.a: The teacher might have felt disappointed but also saw a chance to teach a better way.

grounding: An elder recalls cramming a poem in one night and forgetting it in days, then learning with daily practice.

passage: The night before Republic Day practice, the wedding band next door was blasting, and Lalit had one evening to learn the whole poem, twelve lines. He paced the roof with a torch, shouting the lines over the drums, until he could say them without the paper. At practice next morning he was perfect. Sabina Ma'am clapped. But the real function was four days later. On stage, in front of the whole school, Lalit reached line five and his mind went white, like a wiped slate. He stared at the flag. Sabina Ma'am whispered the next word from the side. Afterwards, red-faced, he said, "I knew it! I knew it on Monday!" She nodded. "You learned it in one night. Next time, a little every day."

qa.q: How many lines did the poem have?
qa.a: Twelve lines.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel after the function?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and frustrated, red-faced, because he had known the poem perfectly on Monday and couldn't see why it vanished.

qa.q: What could Lalit try for the next recitation?
qa.a: Practise a little every day for several days instead of learning it all in one noisy evening.

qa.q: What might Sabina Ma'am have felt when Lalit froze?
qa.a: She was probably worried for him and kind, whispering the next word, and she understood that one-night learning was the cause.

grounding: A boy learns a poem in one evening and has forgotten part of it by the day he needs it.

passage: Two weeks before Christmas, the Aizawl colony was full of fairy lights and choir practice. Chandrika's class had to recite a Hindi poem at the school concert. Her friend Lalremsiami practised it a few lines each evening on the way home, saying it to the stray dogs and the lampposts. Chandrika laughed at her. "I'll learn it in one go," she said, and on Sunday night she sat up with a cup of cocoa and drilled it until she knew every word. On Monday she recited it flawlessly. On Friday, at the dress rehearsal, she stumbled in the second verse and then stopped completely. Lalremsiami carried on, steady and clear. Chandrika stared at her shoes, confused. "It was all there on Monday," she whispered.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami practise the poem?
qa.a: On the way home each evening, saying it to the stray dogs and the lampposts.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling at the dress rehearsal?
qa.a: She felt confused and ashamed, staring at her shoes, because the poem she knew perfectly on Monday had slipped away.

qa.q: What worked for Lalremsiami, and why?
qa.a: Practising a few lines each evening spread the learning over days, so it lasted longer than Chandrika's one-night drill.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel when Chandrika stumbles?
qa.a: She may feel sorry for her friend, and perhaps quietly glad that her slow practice held up.

grounding: A child who learns a poem in one evening forgets it within days, while a friend who practised a little daily remembers it.

passage:
"Vidya didi, test me! The Baisakhi poem. I learned it all last night."
"All sixteen lines? In one night?"
"Yes! Listen." Jasleen rattled it off, perfect.
"Wow. Okay. When's the programme?"
"Next Saturday."
"That's a whole week. Want to practise a bit each day with me?"
"No need. I know it."
Five days later:
"Didi... how does the third verse start?"
"You tell me."
"Something about... the wheat? The fields? I KNEW it!"
"You did know it. For a day or two."
"Why did it run away?"
"Stuffing it all in at once is like pouring water on sand. Little by little, it soaks in."
"Can we practise every day till Saturday?"
"Every single day."

qa.q: When was the Baisakhi programme?
qa.a: Next Saturday.

qa.q: Why does Jasleen shout "I KNEW it!"?
qa.a: Jasleen feels frustrated and upset, having been sure the poem was learned after one night, and now the third verse has slipped away.

qa.q: What plan did they end up with, and why is it better?
qa.a: Practising every day until Saturday; spreading practice over several days makes it last longer than one night of cramming.

qa.q: How does Vidya didi see Jasleen's one-night learning?
qa.a: Vidya expected it to fade, offered daily practice, and stays patient rather than saying "I told you so".

grounding: A child who learns a poem in one night forgets part of it within days and then chooses spaced daily practice.

passage:
The night before our Republic Day practice, I learned the whole poem, all four verses, in one evening. I said it to Mummy ten times. I'm Shreya, and I was so proud.
At practice I said it perfectly, and Ma'am clapped. But the real function was four days later, on the 26th. That morning I stood on the stage, looked out at all the flags, and the second verse was just... gone. Blank. Amandeep whispered it from the side and I finished, but my face was hot.
Amandeep had practised a little bit every day for two weeks. He didn't forget a single word.
Next time I'm doing it his way. A little every day.

qa.q: How many verses did the poem have?
qa.a: Four verses.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel on stage when the second verse vanished?
qa.a: Shreya felt embarrassed and panicky, face hot, after being so proud of learning it in one evening.

qa.q: What could Shreya do differently next time?
qa.a: Practise a little every day for a couple of weeks, the way Amandeep did, instead of all in one evening.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt whispering the verse from the side?
qa.a: He was probably worried and glad to help, and felt steady because his own practice had been spread out.

grounding: Shows a child who learns a poem in one evening and loses part of it within days, unlike a friend who practised a little every day.
